subject: Climate & Environment
title: Slums and Informal Settlements
description: A fast breakdown of Slums and Informal Settlements for builders.

hook.text: Over 1 billion people live in slums — dense, underserved neighborhoods without basic services.

buildup.text: Informal settlements lack clean water, sewage systems, and electricity. Fires and floods are common.

discovery.text: Despite hardship, slums are engines of innovation. Residents build businesses with almost nothing.

twist.text: Upgrading slums — instead of demolishing them — preserves communities while adding infrastructure.

climax.text: Medellín, Colombia transformed its poorest hillside neighborhoods with cable cars and public parks.

punchline.text: A billion people don't need new cities. They need their neighborhoods to work.

quiz.question: How many people live in slums worldwide?

details.summary: Over a billion people live in informal settlements with inadequate housing, sanitation, and services. These communities are highly vulnerable to flooding, heat, and disease. Upgrading them with resilient infrastructure, secure tenure, and basic services is essential for equitable climate adaptation.
details.whyItMatters: Informal settlements are where climate impacts hit hardest. Ignoring them undermines any city's climate resilience and deepens inequality.
takeaways: Over a billion people live in informal urban settlements
Residents face acute exposure to floods, heat, and pollution
Upgrading beats displacement for equitable climate action

faq.question: Why are informal settlements so vulnerable to climate impacts?
faq.answer: They are often built on flood-prone land, steep slopes, or riverbanks. Structures are fragile, drainage is poor, and residents lack insurance or savings to recover from disasters. Limited access to healthcare compounds heat and disease risks.

faq.question: What does effective slum upgrading look like?
faq.answer: Successful programs provide secure land tenure, improved water and sanitation, paved pathways, drainage, and electricity while keeping communities in place. Participatory design involving residents ensures solutions match real needs and builds local ownership.
